html:
Kerma was the first great kingdom of Nubia, centred on the city of Kerma near the Third Cataract of the Nile, in what is now northern Sudan. It grew from about 2500 BCE and reached its peak between about 1750 and 1500 BCE, when it was a rival to Egypt.

The Egyptians called it Kush. Its people were a mix of Nile valley, Saharan and African peoples, and its culture was its own. At the capital stood the Western Deffufa, a huge mud-brick temple that still rises some 18 metres. Its kings were buried under great round mounds with hundreds of sacrificed servants, and with fine thin black-topped pottery.

Its power rested on trade. Gold, ivory, ebony and incense from further south passed through Kerma on their way to Egypt. During the Middle Kingdom Egypt built a chain of forts in Lower Nubia to control this trade and to guard against Kerma.

When Egypt split in the Second Intermediate Period, Kerma took over Lower Nubia and the forts. It allied with the Hyksos in the north; an Egyptian king captured a Hyksos letter inviting the king of Kush to attack Egypt from the south. Kerma raided deep into Egypt, carrying back statues.

The kings of the New Kingdom took revenge. Thutmose I destroyed the city around 1500 BCE (Egypt conquers Kush), and Nubia was ruled from Egypt for some 450 years. Rebellions went on, and from the 11th century BCE a new state rose, the Egyptian-influenced Kingdom of Kush of Napata and Meroë.
